claim: Central vestibular neurons displayed large and highly variable resting discharge rates (51.1 ± 2.8 sp/s; CV*=0.44 ± 0.03) in the absence of stimulation.
source: We found that central neurons displayed large and highly variable resting discharge rates (51.1 ± 2.8 sp/s; CV*=0.44 ± 0.03) in the absence of stimulation, consistent with prior characterizations (e.g. Massot et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct measurements of resting discharge rates and variability from recorded central vestibular neurons.

claim: Regular afferents displayed high resting discharge rates (102.4 ± 6.7 sp/s) and low variability (CV*=0.06 ± 0.005).
source: Notably, regular and irregular afferents displayed high resting discharge rates (regular: 102.4 ± 6.7 sp/s; irregular: 93.7 ± 8.9 sp/s), consistent with previous studies (e.g. Sadeghi et al., 2007a).
evidence: Direct measurements from recordings of regular afferents, with comparison to previous studies.

claim: Irregular afferents displayed high resting discharge rates (93.7 ± 8.9 sp/s) and high variability (CV*=0.33 ± 0.05).
source: Notably, regular and irregular afferents displayed high resting discharge rates (regular: 102.4 ± 6.7 sp/s; irregular: 93.7 ± 8.9 sp/s), consistent with previous studies (e.g. Sadeghi et al., 2007a).
evidence: Direct measurements from recordings of irregular afferents.

claim: The power spectra of naturalistic self-motion signals decayed by more than two orders of magnitude over the frequency range 0–20 Hz.
source: Because the power spectra of these signals decayed by more than two orders of magnitude over the frequency range 0–20 Hz (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), we restricted our analysis to this frequency range.
evidence: Analysis of power spectra from naturalistic stimuli shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Central vestibular neurons showed robust responses to naturalistic self-motion stimuli.
source: We found that central vestibular neurons showed robust responses to naturalistic self-motion stimuli (Figure 1D, bottom panels).
evidence: Neuronal recordings during naturalistic stimulation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The response power spectrum of central vestibular neurons was constant for frequencies within the physiologically relevant range (0–20 Hz).
source: Indeed, the response power spectrum was constant for frequencies within the physiologically relevant range (0–20 Hz; Huterer and Cullen, 2002; Carriot et al., 2017).
evidence: Analysis of response power spectra from central vestibular neurons, with reference to physiologically relevant frequency range from prior studies.

claim: The stimulus power spectrum strongly decayed with increasing frequency.
source: In contrast, the stimulus power spectrum strongly decayed with increasing frequency (Figure 1E, black curve).
evidence: Analysis of stimulus power spectrum shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Response whitening index values for central vestibular neurons were significantly higher than those obtained from the stimulus (p < 0.001).
source: The response whitening index values were significantly higher than those obtained from the stimulus (Figure 1F, left panel of top right inset; p < 0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of whitening indices between neural responses and stimulus.

claim: Response correlation times for central vestibular neurons were significantly lower than those of the stimulus (p < 0.001).
source: Correspondingly, in the temporal domain, the response autocorrelation function decayed to zero faster than that of the stimulus (Figure 1F, bottom inset, compare green and black curves, respectively), as quantified by significantly lower correlations times (Figure 1F, right panel of top right inset; p < 0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation times between neural responses and stimulus.

claim: Central vestibular neurons optimally encode natural self-motion stimuli through whitening.
source: Thus, taken together, our results show that central vestibular neurons optimally encode natural self-motion stimuli through whitening.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from analysis of response power spectra and correlation times.

claim: Regular afferents showed robust responses to naturalistic self-motion stimuli.
source: We found that, while regular and irregular afferents showed robust responses to naturalistic self-motion stimuli (Figure 2B, left and right panels, respectively), neither optimally encode naturalistic self-motion stimuli as their power spectra were not independent of frequency (Figure 2C,D,E,F).
evidence: Neuronal recordings from regular afferents during naturalistic stimulation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Irregular afferents showed robust responses to naturalistic self-motion stimuli.
source: We found that, while regular and irregular afferents showed robust responses to naturalistic self-motion stimuli (Figure 2B, left and right panels, respectively), neither optimally encode naturalistic self-motion stimuli as their power spectra were not independent of frequency (Figure 2C,D,E,F).
evidence: Neuronal recordings from irregular afferents during naturalistic stimulation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Neither regular nor irregular afferents optimally encode naturalistic self-motion stimuli as their power spectra were not independent of frequency.
source: We found that, while regular and irregular afferents showed robust responses to naturalistic self-motion stimuli (Figure 2B, left and right panels, respectively), neither optimally encode naturalistic self-motion stimuli as their power spectra were not independent of frequency (Figure 2C,D,E,F).
evidence: Analysis of power spectra from regular and irregular afferents shown in Figures 2C-F.

claim: The population-averaged response whitening index value for regular afferents was slightly larger than that of the stimulus (p < 0.001).
source: The population-averaged response whitening index value was slightly larger than that of the stimulus (Figure 2D, left panel of top right inset; p < 0.001) but still much smaller than that computed for central vestibular neurons (compare with Figure 1E, left panel of top right inset).
evidence: Statistical comparison of whitening indices for regular afferents versus stimulus.

claim: The population-averaged response correlation time value for regular afferents was not significantly different than that of the stimulus (p = 0.79).
source: Further, the population-averaged response correlation time value was not significantly different than that of the stimulus (Figure 2D, right panel of top right inset; p = 0.79).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation times for regular afferents versus stimulus.

claim: Regular afferents do not perform whitening of natural self-motion stimuli.
source: Thus, our results indicate that, unlike central vestibular neurons, regular afferents do not perform whitening of natural self-motion stimuli.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from analysis of power spectra and correlation times of regular afferents.

claim: The whitening index for irregular afferents was significantly higher than that of the stimulus (p < 0.001).
source: The whitening index was significantly higher than that of the stimulus (Student's t-test, p < 0.001, t(11)=2.25).
evidence: Statistical comparison of whitening indices for irregular afferents versus stimulus, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The correlation time for irregular afferents was significantly lower than that of the stimulus (p < 0.001).
source: The correlation time was significantly lower than that of the stimulus (Student's t-test, p < 0.001, t(11)=9.64).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation times for irregular afferents versus stimulus, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Irregular afferents did not perform whitening of natural self-motion stimuli, as their response power spectra were not constant as a function of frequency.
source: Thus, our results indicate that, like regular afferents but unlike central vestibular neurons, irregular afferents did not perform whitening of natural self-motion stimuli, as their response power spectra were not constant as a function of frequency.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from analysis of power spectra of irregular afferents.

claim: Whitening of natural self-motion by central vestibular neurons is not simply inherited from their afferent input.
source: Therefore, whitening of natural self-motion by central vestibular neurons is not simply inherited from their afferent input.
evidence: Comparison of whitening properties between central neurons and afferents.

claim: Whitening index values for central vestibular neurons were significantly higher than those for either class of afferents (p < 0.01).
source: Comparison of the population-averaged whitening indices (Figure 3B) revealed that significantly higher values for central vestibular neurons than for either class of afferents (p < 0.01; Figure 3B).
evidence: Statistical comparison of whitening indices across neuron types shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Whitening index values for irregular afferents were significantly higher than those for regular afferents (p = 0.002).
source: However, we found that whitening index values for irregular afferents were significantly higher than those for their regular counterparts (p = 0.002; Figure 3B).
evidence: Statistical comparison of whitening indices between irregular and regular afferents shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Population-averaged correlation times for central vestibular neurons were lower than for either class of afferents (regular: p < 0.001; irregular: p = 0.004).
source: Consistent with our spectral analysis above, population-averaged correlation times for central vestibular neurons were lower than for either class of afferents (regular: p < 0.001; irregular: p = 0.004; Figure 3D), while correlation times for irregular afferents were significantly lower than those of regular afferents (p = 0.006; Figure 3D).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation times across neuron types shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Correlation times for irregular afferents were significantly lower than those of regular afferents (p = 0.006).
source: Consistent with our spectral analysis above, population-averaged correlation times for central vestibular neurons were lower than for either class of afferents (regular: p < 0.001; irregular: p = 0.004; Figure 3D), while correlation times for irregular afferents were significantly lower than those of regular afferents (p = 0.006; Figure 3D).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation times between irregular and regular afferents shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Whitening occurs in stages: some decorrelation of naturalistic self-motion input is achieved by irregular afferents and further decorrelation occurs at the level of central vestibular neurons.
source: Thus, we conclude that whitening occurs in stages: some decorrelation of naturalistic self-motion input is achieved by irregular afferents and further decorrelation of this input occurs as the level of central vestibular neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of whitening and correlation times across neuron types.

claim: Predicted whitening index values from tuning alone were consistently lower than actual values for central vestibular neurons (p < 0.001).
source: Quantification of our results showed that predicted whitening index values were consistently lower than actual values (p < 0.001; Figure 4C).
evidence: Statistical comparison between predicted and actual whitening indices shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Whitening by central vestibular neurons could not be accounted for by static nonlinearities.
source: Further, whitening by central vestibular neurons could not be accounted for by static nonlinearities (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2; see Materials and methods), or by their tuning to artificial sinusoidal stimulation at discrete frequencies (Figure 5, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Analysis of nonlinear models shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The tuning functions of both regular and irregular afferents were sufficient to predict their response power spectra to naturalistic self-motion.
source: In contrast, the tuning functions of both regular and irregular afferents were sufficient to predict their response power spectra to naturalistic self-motion (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), thereby showing that greater temporal whitening of naturalistic self-motion stimuli by irregular afferents is due to their greater high-pass tuning properties.
evidence: Analysis of afferent tuning and response predictions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Greater temporal whitening of naturalistic self-motion stimuli by irregular afferents is due to their greater high-pass tuning properties.
source: In contrast, the tuning functions of both regular and irregular afferents were sufficient to predict their response power spectra to naturalistic self-motion (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), thereby showing that greater temporal whitening of naturalistic self-motion stimuli by irregular afferents is due to their greater high-pass tuning properties.
evidence: Inference from comparison of tuning properties and whitening between regular and irregular afferents.

claim: The tuning function of central vestibular neurons does not fully compensate for the decaying power spectrum of natural self-motion stimuli and thus cannot account for their whitened responses.
source: Thus, we conclude that the tuning function of central vestibular neurons does not fully compensate for the decaying power spectrum of natural self-motion stimuli and thus cannot account for their whitened responses.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of predicted and actual response power spectra.

claim: The response power spectrum is equal to the sum of the noise power spectrum and the power spectrum of the response predicted by tuning alone.
source: Specifically, the response power spectrum is equal to the sum of the noise power spectrum (i.e. the power spectrum of the neural variability) and the power spectrum of the response that would be predicted by tuning alone (i.e. transmitted power; Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Theoretical framework illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: To maximize information through whitening, it is the response power spectrum that should be constant as a function of frequency, rather than the transmitted power spectrum.
source: Thus, in order to maximize information through whitening, it is the response power spectrum that should be constant as a function of frequency, rather than the transmitted power spectrum.
evidence: Theoretical prediction from information theory.

claim: For a given noise intensity and spectrum, varying the transmitted power spectrum can have significant influence on mutual information.
source: Thus, our results show that, for a given noise intensity and spectrum, varying the transmitted power spectrum can have significant influence on mutual information.
evidence: Conclusion from modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B-D.

claim: With increasing noise intensity, mutual information decreases.
source: We found that, with increasing noise intensity, noise as well as response power increased uniformly for all frequencies (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E,F), but that mutual information decreased (Figure 4—figure supplement 4G).
evidence: Modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E-G.

claim: To maximize information, the spectral frequency content of the neural variability should perfectly compensate the transmitted power, such that the sum of the two is constant as a function of frequency.
source: Specifically, to maximize information, the spectral frequency content of the neural variability should perfectly compensate the transmitted power, such that the sum of the two is constant as a function of frequency.
evidence: Conclusion from modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The resting discharge power spectrum of central vestibular neurons increases at higher frequencies.
source: We found that the resting discharge power spectrum increases at higher frequencies (Figure 6B, inset, black curve) and thus, in conjunction with the neural tuning function (Figure 4B, inset), effectively compensated for decaying stimulus power.
evidence: Analysis of resting discharge power spectrum shown in Figure 6B inset.

claim: The resting discharge power spectrum, in conjunction with the neural tuning function, effectively compensated for decaying stimulus power in central vestibular neurons.
source: We found that the resting discharge power spectrum increases at higher frequencies (Figure 6B, inset, black curve) and thus, in conjunction with the neural tuning function (Figure 4B, inset), effectively compensated for decaying stimulus power.
evidence: Analysis combining resting discharge and tuning to predict response power spectrum.

claim: Predicted and actual response power spectra for central vestibular neurons were in excellent agreement when using both resting discharge and tuning.
source: Indeed, the predicted and actual response power spectra were in excellent agreement (Figure 6B, compare green and light green curves).
evidence: Comparison of predicted and actual response power spectra shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Predicted and actual whitening index values for central vestibular neurons were not significantly different from one another (p = 0.39) when using both resting discharge and tuning.
source: Further, predicted and actual whitening index values were not significantly different from one another (p = 0.39; Figure 6C).
evidence: Statistical comparison of predicted and actual whitening indices shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The power spectrum of the resting discharge and the residual (trial-to-trial variability) were quite similar for central vestibular neurons.
source: We found that the power spectrum of the resting discharge and the residual were quite similar (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), thus validating our assumption that the power spectrum of the resting discharge can be used to estimate that of the trial-to-trial variability during stimulation.
evidence: Comparison of resting discharge and residual power spectra shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Actual information rates transmitted by central vestibular neurons were in good agreement with optimal values.
source: We found that actual information rates transmitted by central vestibular neurons were in good agreement with optimal values (Figure 6D, left panel), and comparison with afferents revealed that the actual information rate of central vestibular neurons was significantly closer to its maximum possible value (Figure 6D, right panel and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparison of actual and optimal information rates shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The actual information rate of central vestibular neurons was significantly closer to its maximum possible value compared to afferents.
source: We found that actual information rates transmitted by central vestibular neurons were in good agreement with optimal values (Figure 6D, left panel), and comparison with afferents revealed that the actual information rate of central vestibular neurons was significantly closer to its maximum possible value (Figure 6D, right panel and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical comparison of normalized information rates shown in Figure 6D right panel.

claim: Due to their higher variability, information rates computed from central vestibular neurons were lower than those of afferents.
source: Moreover, our modeling correctly predicted that, due to their higher variability, information rates computed from central vestibular neurons were lower than those of afferents (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparison of information rates shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2, consistent with modeling predictions.

claim: The experimentally observed whitening by central vestibular neurons is achieved because both the power spectra of their variability and their tuning function effectively compensate for the decaying power of natural self-motion.
source: Thus, we conclude that the experimentally observed whitening by central vestibular neurons is achieved because both the power spectra of their variability and their tuning function effectively compensate for the decaying power of natural self-motion.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from analysis combining tuning and variability to predict whitened responses.

claim: The power spectrum of neural variability can have important consequences on determining whether sensory neurons optimally encode natural stimuli.
source: Taken together, our findings show that the power spectrum of neural variability can have important consequences on determining whether sensory neurons optimally encode natural stimuli; thereby overturning the prevailing view that whitening is achieved by neural tuning alone.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings showing the role of variability in whitening.

claim: The brain's neural coding strategies are adapted to the statistics of natural stimuli.
source: It is commonly assumed that the brain's neural coding strategies are adapted to the statistics of natural stimuli.
evidence: Statement of commonly held assumption in neuroscience.

claim: To maximize information transmission, a sensory neuron's tuning function should effectively oppose the decaying stimulus spectral power, such that the neural response is temporally decorrelated.
source: Specifically, to maximize information transmission, a sensory neuron's tuning function should effectively oppose the decaying stimulus spectral power, such that the neural response is temporally decorrelated (i.e. 'whitened').
evidence: Statement of prevailing theoretical view in neuroscience.

claim: Theory predicts that the structure of neuronal variability plays an essential role in determining how coding is optimized.
source: However, theory predicts that the structure of neuronal variability also plays an essential role in determining how coding is optimized.
evidence: Statement of theoretical prediction.

claim: Neuronal variability and tuning were matched to effectively complement natural stimulus statistics, thereby achieving temporal decorrelation and optimizing information transmission in central vestibular neurons.
source: Rather, computational modeling and analysis revealed that neuronal variability and tuning were matched to effectively complement natural stimulus statistics, thereby achieving temporal decorrelation and optimizing information transmission.
evidence: Conclusion from computational modeling and experimental analysis.

claim: During everyday life, the inputs to our sensory systems have clearly defined statistical structures characterized by a pronounced decay in spectral power with increasing frequency.
source: During everyday life, the inputs to our sensory systems have clearly defined statistical structures characterized by a pronounced decay in spectral power with increasing frequency (visual and auditory systems as reviewed in: Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; vestibular system: Carriot et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work in multiple sensory systems.

claim: Sensory pathways are adapted to the statistical properties of natural stimuli.
source: It is generally agreed that sensory pathways are adapted to the statistical properties of natural stimuli (Laughlin, 1981; Attneave, 1954; Barlow, 1961; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; Olshausen and Field, 2004; Wark et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement of general agreement in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The brain optimizes information transmission by removing the redundancy of time-varying input, such that the spectral power of the resulting neuronal response is constant.
source: In this context, the brain is thought to optimize information transmission by removing the redundancy of (i.e. decorrelate) time-varying input, such that the spectral power of the resulting neuronal response is constant (i.e. are 'whitened'; Srinivasan et al., 1982; Atick and Redlich, 1990; Atick, 2011).
evidence: Statement of theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: Whitening has been reported in several early sensory pathways.
source: Indeed, the fact that whitening has been reported in several early sensory pathways supports this idea (Dan et al., 1996; Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The prevailing view is that whitening at the single neuron level is achieved as a result of a precise match between tuning and stimulus statistics.
source: The prevailing view is that whitening at the single neuron level is achieved as a result of a precise match between tuning and stimulus statistics.
evidence: Statement of prevailing view in the field.

claim: High-pass tuning is thought to be mediated by intrinsic cellular dynamics that give rise to spike frequency adaptation and/or other mechanisms such as synaptic plasticity.
source: Such high-pass tuning is thought to be mediated by intrinsic cellular dynamics that give rise to spike frequency adaptation (Benda and Herz, 2003; Wang et al., 2003; Pozzorini et al., 2013) and/or other mechanisms such as synaptic plasticity (Jackman and Regehr, 2017).
evidence: Statement of proposed mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: A match between the frequency spectra of neural tuning and stimulus statistics alone will not optimize information transmission.
source: However, in general, a match between the frequency spectra of neural tuning and stimulus statistics alone will not optimize information transmission.
evidence: Statement of theoretical principle.

claim: The structure of the trial-to-trial variability of the neural response can strongly influence optimal coding.
source: This is because the structure of the trial-to-trial variability of the neural response can strongly influence optimal coding as predicted from theory (van Hateren, 1992; Rieke et al., 1996; Tkacik et al., 2008; Tkacik et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement of theoretical prediction supported by citations.

claim: In most brain areas, neural variability is not independent of frequency as it displays significant temporal correlations.
source: Further, in most brain areas, neural variability is not independent of frequency as it displays significant temporal correlations (Jaeger and Bower, 1994; Gershon et al., 1998; Manwani and Koch, 1999; Oram et al., 1999; Goldberg, 2000; Maimon and Assad, 2009; Shinomoto et al., 2009; Massot et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The effects of frequency-dependent structure of trial-to-trial variability on optimal coding at the single neuron level have for the most part been ignored.
source: To date, however, the effects of frequency-dependent structure of trial-to-trial variability on optimal coding at the single neuron level have for the most part been ignored (Field, 1987; Körding et al., 2004; Graham et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2016), not systematically investigated (van Hateren et al., 2002), or found to have minimal effect (Pitkow and Meister, 2012).
evidence: Statement about the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: The fundamental question of whether the frequency spectrum of neuronal variability actively contributes to optimizing information transmission of natural stimuli by sensory neurons has not yet been addressed experimentally.
source: Thus, the fundamental question of whether the frequency spectrum of neuronal variability actively contributes to optimizing information transmission of natural stimuli by sensory neurons has not yet been addressed experimentally.
evidence: Statement about gap in experimental knowledge.

claim: The vestibular system benefits from well-described organization and easily described natural stimuli.
source: The vestibular system benefits from well-described organization and easily described natural stimuli (e.g. head motion as a function of time; Cullen, 2011).
evidence: Statement about the vestibular system supported by citation.

claim: The vestibular system generates reflexes that are vital for gaze and posture stabilization, as well as for accurate spatial perception and motor control.
source: This essential system generates reflexes that are vital for gaze and posture stabilization, as well as for accurate spatial perception and motor control (Cullen, 2012).
evidence: Statement about vestibular system function supported by citation.

claim: Vestibular afferents display a wide range of resting discharge variabilities.
source: Vestibular afferents displaying a wide range of resting discharge variabilities innervate the receptor cells of the vestibular sensors and synapse onto neurons within the central vestibular nuclei.
evidence: Statement about vestibular afferent properties.

claim: Central vestibular neurons project to both motor centers and higher brain areas.
source: These project to both motor centers and higher brain areas (e.g. thalamus; Goldberg, 2000; Cullen, 2012), thereby mediating vital reflexes and self-motion perception, respectively.
evidence: Statement about central vestibular neuron projections supported by citations.

claim: The variability of the resting discharge contributes to determining response variability during stimulation.
source: Indeed, the variability of the resting discharge contributes to determining response variability during stimulation (Ratnam and Nelson, 2000; Chacron et al., 2003; Chacron et al., 2005; Sadeghi et al., 2007a).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Differences in resting discharge variability for afferents and central vestibular neurons strongly influence information transmission about self-motion.
source: In particular, differences in resting discharge variability for afferents and central vestibular neurons strongly influence information transmission about self-motion, as assessed by using artificial (e.g. sinusoidal or noise) stimuli (Sadeghi et al., 2007a; Massot et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Early vestibular pathways demonstrate whitening at the first stage of central processing.
source: We found that early vestibular pathways demonstrate whitening at the first stage of central processing.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental findings.

claim: Whitening is not simply inherited from afferents.
source: Importantly, whitening is not simply inherited from afferents.
evidence: Conclusion from comparison of afferent and central neuron responses.

claim: The tuning properties of central neurons alone do not predict their exceptionally whitened responses to natural self-motion.
source: Additionally, the tuning properties of central neurons alone do not predict their exceptionally whitened responses to natural self-motion.
evidence: Conclusion from comparison of predicted and actual responses.

claim: The frequency spectra of both tuning and variability significantly influence information transmission.
source: By using a computational model, we predicted that the frequency spectra of both tuning and variability will both significantly influence information transmission.
evidence: Prediction from computational modeling.

claim: While increasing the level of variability will decrease information transmission, the frequency spectrum of neural variability for a given level will strongly determine optimality of coding.
source: Notably, while increasing the level of variability will decrease information transmission, the frequency spectrum of neural variability for a given level will strongly determine optimality of coding (i.e. how close is the mutual information to its maximum value).
evidence: Conclusion from modeling and experimental results.

claim: Coding was more optimized in central neurons than in afferents as the mutual information normalized by its maximum value was significantly higher.
source: Indeed, we found that coding was more optimized in central neurons than in afferents as the mutual information normalized by its maximum value was significantly higher.
evidence: Comparison of normalized mutual information between central neurons and afferents.

claim: The trial-to-trial variability during stimulation can be well approximated by that of the resting activity in the absence of stimulation.
source: Theory predicts that the trial-to-trial variability during stimulation can be well approximated by that of the resting activity in the absence of stimulation (Risken, 1996) and our results show that this is the case for central vestibular neurons under naturalistic stimulation.
evidence: Theoretical prediction supported by experimental validation.

claim: The resting rates of central vestibular neurons are lower than those of afferents (~50 sp/s vs. ~100 sp/s, respectively).
source: Further, it has long been known that the resting rates of central vestibular neurons, despite being lower than those of afferents (~50 sp/s vs. ~100 sp/s, respectively), are substantially more variable (Goldberg, 2000; Massot et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement of known fact supported by citations.

claim: The resting rates of central vestibular neurons are substantially more variable than those of afferents.
source: Further, it has long been known that the resting rates of central vestibular neurons, despite being lower than those of afferents (~50 sp/s vs. ~100 sp/s, respectively), are substantially more variable (Goldberg, 2000; Massot et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement of known fact supported by citations.

claim: The power spectrum of the resting discharge can be considered as a 'noise spectrum' as it represents the amount of noise present at each frequency.
source: In particular, the power spectrum of the resting discharge can be considered as a 'noise spectrum' as it represents the amount of noise present at each frequency, and thus can approximate neural variability under stimulation (Ratnam and Nelson, 2000; Chacron et al., 2003; Chacron et al., 2005; Massot et al., 2011; Jamali et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Central vestibular neurons display higher detection thresholds than single afferents.
source: In the vestibular system, the fact that central vestibular neurons display higher levels of resting discharge than afferents thus provides an explanation as to why they display higher detection thresholds, and transmit less information about artificial self-motion stimuli than single afferents (Massot et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Central vestibular neurons transmit less information about artificial self-motion stimuli than single afferents.
source: In the vestibular system, the fact that central vestibular neurons display higher levels of resting discharge than afferents thus provides an explanation as to why they display higher detection thresholds, and transmit less information about artificial self-motion stimuli than single afferents (Massot et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The increased resting discharge variability observed at higher stages of vestibular processing is detrimental to information transmission.
source: Consequently, the increased resting discharge variability observed at higher stages of vestibular processing is detrimental to information transmission.
evidence: Inference from prior findings about information transmission.

claim: The spectral content of neural variability strongly influences information transmission.
source: Importantly, our results show that the spectral content of neural variability strongly influences information transmission.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental and modeling results.

claim: In order to optimize neural coding of natural self-motion stimuli through whitening, it is essential that the spectral frequency content of the resting discharge perfectly compensate the power transmitted from the stimulus.
source: Thus, in order to optimize neural coding of natural self-motion stimuli through whitening, such that response power is constant as a function of frequency, it is essential that the spectral frequency content of the resting discharge perfectly compensate the power transmitted from the stimulus (i.e. the transmitted power, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Conclusion from modeling and experimental results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The higher resting discharge variability of central vestibular neurons decreases information transmission relative to that of afferents.
source: Thus, while the higher resting discharge variability of central vestibular neurons actually decreases information transmission relative to that of afferents (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), the spectral content of this variability is set such as to optimize the information being transmitted since the mutual information for central vestibular neurons is closer to its maximum value than for afferents (Figure 6D).
evidence: Comparison of information transmission shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The spectral content of variability in central vestibular neurons is set such as to optimize the information being transmitted.
source: Thus, while the higher resting discharge variability of central vestibular neurons actually decreases information transmission relative to that of afferents (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), the spectral content of this variability is set such as to optimize the information being transmitted since the mutual information for central vestibular neurons is closer to its maximum value than for afferents (Figure 6D).
evidence: Conclusion from comparison of normalized mutual information shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A match between stimulus statistics, neural tuning, and trial-to-trial variability further optimizes information transmission at the population level.
source: We hypothesize that a match between stimulus statistics, neural tuning, and trial-to-trial variability further optimizes information transmission at the population level as proposed in other systems (Doi et al., 2012; Kastner et al., 2015).
evidence: Hypothesis based on findings in other systems, supported by citations.

claim: Neural variability increases at the level of central neurons relative to that observed in more peripheral areas across multiple systems.
source: Previous studies performed in multiple systems have shown that neural variability actually increases at the level of central neurons relative to that observed in more peripheral areas (visual: Kara et al., 2000; auditory: Wang et al., 2008; electrosensory: Maler, 2009), which is thought to be due to intense synaptic bombardment (Destexhe et al., 2001; Destexhe et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work in multiple systems.

claim: There is a match between the tuning properties and variability of central vestibular neurons which enables optimized encoding of natural self-motion through temporal whitening.
source: Here, we showed that there is a match between the tuning properties and variability of central vestibular neurons which enables optimized encoding of natural self-motion through temporal whitening.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental findings.

claim: The spectral frequency content of neural variability is matched to that of the tuning function to optimize encoding of natural stimuli.
source: This result constitutes an experimental demonstration that the spectral frequency content of neural variability is matched to that of the tuning function to optimize encoding of natural stimuli, as predicted by theoretical studies (Rieke et al., 1996).
evidence: Conclusion from experimental findings, with reference to theoretical predictions.

claim: Most previous studies have focused on tuning and either assumed that neural variability was negligible or did not display temporal correlations.
source: Indeed, most previous studies have focused on tuning and either assumed that neural variability was negligible or did not display temporal correlations (Dan et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2003; Pitkow and Meister, 2012).
evidence: Statement about prior work supported by citations.

claim: Neurons displaying large and variable spontaneous activity with temporal correlations are found ubiquitously within the sensory periphery and central brain regions.
source: However, neurons displaying large and variable spontaneous activity (i.e. resting discharge activity) with temporal correlations are found ubiquitously within the sensory periphery and central brain regions (Hubel, 1959; Evarts, 1964; Pfeiffer and Kiang, 1965; Steriade et al., 1978; Jaeger and Bower, 1994; Köppl, 1997; Aizenman and Linden, 1999; Schneidman et al., 2006; Greschner et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations across different brain regions and systems.

claim: Neural variability, together with tuning, plays a fundamental role towards optimizing information transmission about natural stimuli, and this will be generally applicable across sensory systems and species.
source: Accordingly, we speculate that our results showing that neural variability, together with tuning, plays a fundamental role towards optimizing information transmission about natural stimuli, will be generally applicable across sensory systems and species.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings and ubiquity of variable neurons.

claim: Under natural conditions, vestibular stimulation results from both active and passive self-motion.
source: However, it is important to note that, under natural conditions, vestibular stimulation results from both active and passive self-motion.
evidence: Statement about natural vestibular stimulation.

claim: Afferents respond similarly to both active and passive self-motion stimuli.
source: Previous studies have established that afferents respond similarly to both classes of stimuli (Cullen and Minor, 2002; Sadeghi et al., 2007b; Jamali et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: VO neurons display markedly attenuated responses to active self-motion consisting of head and/or body orienting movements.
source: However, the central vestibular neurons which were the focus of the present study (i.e. VO neurons) display markedly attenuated responses to active self-motion consisting of head and/or body orienting movements (reviewed in: Cullen, 2012) due to integration of vestibular and extra-vestibular (e.g., proprioceptive and motor) signals.
evidence: Statement about VO neuron properties supported by citation.

claim: Natural self-motion stimuli generally comprise of both three-dimensional rotational and translational components.
source: We further note that natural self-motion stimuli are generally not restricted to one axis of motion, but rather comprise of both three-dimensional rotational and translational components (Carriot et al., 2014; Carriot et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about natural self-motion supported by citations.

claim: Three male macaque monkeys were used in the experiments.
source: Three male macaque monkeys (2 Macaca mulatta and 1 Macaca fascicularis) were prepared for chronic extracellular recording using aseptic surgical techniques as previously described (Massot et al., 2011).
evidence: Description of experimental subjects.

claim: Animals were aged 7, 8, and 8 years old.
source: Animals (aged 7, 8, and 8 years old) were housed in pairs on a 12 hr light/dark cycle.
evidence: Description of experimental subjects.

claim: The resting discharge regularity of vestibular afferents displays a bimodal distribution, which defines two afferent classes, regular and irregular.
source: In particular, the resting discharge regularity of vestibular afferents displays a bimodal distribution, which defines two afferent classes, regular and irregular, further characterized by differences in axon diameter as well as response dynamics (reviewed in: Goldberg, 2000; Eatock et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement about afferent classification supported by citations.

claim: A bimodal distribution of CV* values was found for the afferent dataset (Hartigan's Dip Test; p = 0.002).
source: We found a bimodal distribution of CV* values for our data set (Hartigan's Dip Test; p = 0.002) and thus classified afferents with CV*<0.1 as regular and as irregular otherwise, as done previously (Goldberg et al., 1984).
evidence: Statistical test of CV* distribution from experimental data.

claim: Afferents with CV*<0.1 were classified as regular.
source: We found a bimodal distribution of CV* values for our data set (Hartigan's Dip Test; p = 0.002) and thus classified afferents with CV*<0.1 as regular and as irregular otherwise, as done previously (Goldberg et al., 1984).
evidence: Classification criterion applied to experimental data, based on prior work.

claim: The probability distributions of naturalistic stimuli were well-fit by a Gaussian.
source: We found that that the probability distributions of these signals were well-fit by a Gaussian (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of stimulus distributions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The probability distributions of firing rate during naturalistic stimuli were well-fit by a Gaussian.
source: We found that that the probability distributions of these signals were well-fit by a Gaussian (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of firing rate distributions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Horizontal canal afferents only respond to the component of rotational self-motion along the yaw axis.
source: We note that, while horizontal canal afferents only respond to the component of rotational self-motion along the yaw axis (Fernandez and Goldberg, 1971), this is not the case for central vestibular neurons.
evidence: Statement about afferent response properties supported by citation.

claim: Central vestibular neurons integrate inputs from multiple canal and otoliths in a manner that is both nonlinear and frequency dependent.
source: Indeed, these neurons integrate inputs from multiple canal and otoliths in a manner that is both nonlinear and frequency dependent (Dickman and Angelaki, 2002; Carriot et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about central neuron properties supported by citations.

claim: All experimental protocols were approved by the McGill University Animal Care Committee and were in compliance with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care.
source: All experimental protocols were approved by the McGill University Animal Care Committee and were in compliance with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.

claim: Recordings were made from 27 central vestibular-only (VO) neurons.
source: We recorded from central vestibular-only (VO) neurons within the vestibular nuclei (VN) that are responsive to rotational head motion but not eye movements (n = 27).
evidence: Description of experimental sample size.

claim: Recordings were made from 14 regular afferents.
source: For comparison, recordings were also made directly from individual semicircular canal afferents that were classified as either regular (n = 14; CV*=0.06 ± 0.005) or irregular (n = 12; CV*=0.33 ± 0.05) based on a previously established bimodal distribution of resting discharge variability corresponding to differences in axon diameter, response dynamics, and response sensitivity (Goldberg, 2000; Sadeghi et al., 2007a; Eatock et al., 2008; Massot et al., 2011; Massot et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of experimental sample size.

claim: Recordings were made from 12 irregular afferents.
source: For comparison, recordings were also made directly from individual semicircular canal afferents that were classified as either regular (n = 14; CV*=0.06 ± 0.005) or irregular (n = 12; CV*=0.33 ± 0.05) based on a previously established bimodal distribution of resting discharge variability corresponding to differences in axon diameter, response dynamics, and response sensitivity (Goldberg, 2000; Sadeghi et al., 2007a; Eatock et al., 2008; Massot et al., 2011; Massot et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of experimental sample size.

claim: Central vestibular VO neurons receive direct synaptic input from vestibular afferents and project to higher brain areas mediating self-motion perception.
source: These neurons receive direct synaptic input from vestibular afferents, and project to higher brain areas mediating self-motion perception (Figure 1A; reviewed in: Cullen, 2012).
evidence: Statement about VO neuron connectivity supported by citation and shown in Figure 1A.
